3.note: The expression **you will be captured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to state who will do the action, the context indicates that it will be the soldiers of the king of Babylon. Alternate translation: [the soldiers of the king of Babylon will certainly capture you]

The expression **you will be given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to state who will do the action, the context indicates that Yahweh will do it by means of the army of the king of Babylon. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will give you into his hand]

3.q: וְֽ֠⁠עֵינֶי⁠ךָ אֶת עֵינֵ֨י מֶֽלֶךְ בָּבֶ֜ל תִּרְאֶ֗ינָה
3.note: Here, **your eyes will see the eyes of the king of Babylon** means “you will meet the king of Babylon face to face.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And you will personally face the king of Babylon]

Here, **his mouth will speak with your mouth** means “he will speak with you directly.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he will speak to you personally]

Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **capture** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you will certainly be captured]

4.note: Here, **the sword** represents “battle” or a violent death in war. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [You will not be killed in war]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:4.

5.q: וּֽ⁠כְ⁠מִשְׂרְפ֣וֹת אֲ֠בוֹתֶי⁠ךָ הַ⁠מְּלָכִ֨ים הָ⁠רִֽאשֹׁנִ֜ים אֲשֶׁר־הָי֣וּ לְ⁠פָנֶ֗י⁠ךָ כֵּ֚ן יִשְׂרְפוּ־לָ֔⁠ךְ
5.note: The point of this comparison is that just as there were **burnings** of spices to honor Zedekiah’s ancestors, the kings of Judah, when they died, so people will burn spices to honor Zedekiah when he dies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and just as people burned spices to honor your ancestors when they died, the former kings who were before you, so they will burn spices or you]

Yahweh is not distinguishing these **former kings** from other former kings who were not **before** Zedekiah. Yahweh is reminding Zedekiah that these ancestors of his were the kings who ruled Judah before him. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [who were the kings who ruled before you]

5.q: כֵּ֚ן יִשְׂרְפוּ לָ֔⁠ךְ וְ⁠ה֥וֹי אָד֖וֹן יִסְפְּדוּ לָ֑⁠ךְ
5.note: The pronoun **they** refers to Zedekiah’s people, who will honor him and mourn for him when he dies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [so your people will burn for you, “Alas, master!” your people will mourn for you]

The people mourning for Zedekiah will be using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of grief. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how we grieve for you, master]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I have spoken** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself has promised this, so Zedekiah can be sure that it will happen. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I have certainly promised this]

8.note: Jeremiah is using the phrase translated as **The word that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

Jeremiah is using **cut a covenant** as a common expression of the culture to mean “made a covenant.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verses 13, 15, and 18. This also occurs in verse 15. Alternate translation: [King Zedekiah made a covenant]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **freedom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to proclaim that they would be set free]

9.q: לְ֠⁠שַׁלַּח אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־עַבְדּ֞⁠וֹ וְ⁠אִ֧ישׁ אֶת־שִׁפְחָת֛⁠וֹ הָ⁠עִבְרִ֥י וְ⁠הָ⁠עִבְרִיָּ֖ה חָפְשִׁ֑ים
9.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [each man must send away his male and female Hebrew slaves]

Jeremiah is using **to not serve by them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “so that no one would make them serve as slaves.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 10. Alternate translation: [so that no one would keep them as slaves]

Jeremiah is using the term **brother** to describe people who are descended from the same ancestor. Here it means a fellow Israelite. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verses 14 and 17. Alternate translation: [on a Jew, his fellow Israelite]

Jeremiah is using **a man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “each man.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each man his male servant and each man his female servant]

17.q: הִנְ⁠נִ֣י קֹרֵא֩ לָ⁠כֶ֨ם דְּר֜וֹר נְאֻם יְהוָ֗ה אֶל הַ⁠חֶ֨רֶב֙ אֶל הַ⁠דֶּ֣בֶר וְ⁠אֶל הָ⁠רָעָ֔ב
17.note: Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of the phrase ** proclaiming freedom to you**. The people would not give **freedom** to their slaves, so the only freedom that Yahweh will give the people is to die by **the sword**, **the plague**, and **the famine**. If a speaker of your language would express the meaning that way, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold, I will hand you over”—the declaration of Yahweh—“to die by the sword, by the plague, and by the famine] or [Behold me handing you over”—the declaration of Yahweh—“to die by the sword, by the plague, and by the famine]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:15.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **horror**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will make you horrifying]

18.q: וְ⁠נָתַתִּ֣י אֶת הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֗ים הָ⁠עֹֽבְרִים֙ אֶת בְּרִתִ֔⁠י
18.note: Yahweh begins a sentence here that he does not complete until verse 20, where he says what he will do to these men. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information in verse 20 with the information about **the men transgressing my covenant** here, and then describe these men in a separate sentence. Alternate translation: [And I will give the men transgressing my covenant into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those seeking their life. I will do this to those men who have transgressed my covenant]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the words that stated what the people had promised to do in the covenant. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the words that stated what they had promised in the covenant]

18.q: הָ⁠עֵ֨גֶל֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר כָּרְת֣וּ לִ⁠שְׁנַ֔יִם וַ⁠יַּעַבְר֖וּ בֵּ֥ין בְּתָרָֽי⁠ו
18.note: The implication is that the people had cut a calf in two and walked between the pieces as part of the ceremony of making the covenant. By doing this, they were saying that they should be killed like the calf if they did not keep the covenant. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the calf that they cut in two and passed between its pieces, showing that they deserved to be killed like that calf if they broke the covenant]
